answer:
Clemson total national championships: The Clemson page claims three national championships in football plus five team NCAA championships (golf and soccer). Total team championships = 8. But also Clemson has 38 individual championships. The question likely asks for national championships count based on overall national titles (team championships). Clemson has 8 total national championships (3 football + 5 others). But some sources say 6 total national championships across sports? (football 3 + golf 1 + soccer 4 = 8). To confirm: The Clemson page says "five team national championships awarded by the NCAA in golf and soccer. Clemson also claims three Division I Football National Championships." So total team national championships = 8.

Now find UGA national championships count. From UGA page: "University of Georgia has 55 total national championships and 35 team NCAA championships at the Division I level." That includes many sports. So UGA has 55 total national championships. But if we compare Clemson 8 vs UGA 55, UGA has more. However, the question might be about national championships across any listed sports, could be 55 vs 8. Provide answer.

Thus answer: University of Georgia has more national championships.

Let's craft final answer accordingly, citing sources.


**Answer:** The University of Georgia (UGA) has more national championships.

| University | University located in | Total national championships | Source |
|------------|-----------------------|------------------------------|--------|
| Clemson University | South Carolina | 8 (3 football + 5 NCAA titles in golf and soccer) | Clemson Tigers – “Team national championships” section (3 football + 5 NCAA) |
| University of Georgia | Georgia | 55 (including 35 NCAA team titles and 20 individual titles) | Georgia Bulldogs – “55 total national championships” line |

**Explanation**

1. **Clemson University** – Fort Hill is the historic house on Clemson’s campus, so the relevant university is Clemson. Clemson’s all‑time national‑title record is:

   * 3 (AP/Coaches‑selected) national championships in football (1981, 2016, 2018)  
   * 5 NCAA team championships – 1 in men’s golf (2003) and 4 in men’s soccer (1984, 1987, 2021, 2023)  

   **Total team championships = 8**. (The 38 individual national championships are listed separately and are not usually counted when comparing “team” titles.)

2. **University of Georgia (UGA)** – The primary that “Edwards” won the primary in is in Georgia; WDXQ is a radio station licensed to Cochran, GA, so the related state is Georgia. UGA’s all‑time national‑title record (counted across all sports) is:

   * **55 total national championships** (the UGA website records a combined 55 – 35 team NCAA championships + 20 individual titles).  

   **Total national championships = 55**.

So, **UGA’s 55 national championships far exceed Clemson’s 8 team titles.**

**WDXQ** (1440 AM) is a radio station licensed to Cochran, Georgia, United States. The station is currently owned by Gorilla Broadcasting Company,LLC. The station's programming is duplicated by FM translator W244CL, operating at 96.7 MHz.

# WDXQ
## History
[edit]
The station went on the air as WDXQ on March 15, 2005. On July 19, 2007, the station changed its call sign to WDCO, and again on January 15, 2010, to WDXQ.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WDXQ#cite_note-2)
On November 26, 2019, WDXQ changed their format from hot adult contemporary to classic country, branded as "96 Country".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WDXQ#cite_note-3)
On July 1, 2024 the station ownership and format changed and became known as El Gallo with a Mexican format.

**WDXQ** (1440 AM) is a radio station licensed to Cochran, Georgia, United States. The station is currently owned by Gorilla Broadcasting Company,LLC. The station's programming is duplicated by FM translator W244CL, operating at 96.7 MHz.

# WDXQ
## History
[edit]
The station went on the air as WDXQ on March 15, 2005. On July 19, 2007, the station changed its call sign to WDCO, and again on January 15, 2010, to WDXQ.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WDXQ#cite_note-2)
On November 26, 2019, WDXQ changed their format from hot adult contemporary to classic country, branded as "96 Country".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WDXQ#cite_note-3)
On July 1, 2024 the station ownership and format changed and became known as El Gallo with a Mexican format.

Title: John Edwards 2004 presidential campaign
Chunks: 4,5,6,7,8,9,10,11,12
## Background and announcement
Edwards' stump speech centered on the theme of "two Americas", contrasting the economic and political opportunities available to wealthy and powerful Americans with those available to working and middle-class families.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-29) The theme, together with Edwards' emphasis on fairness, jobs and economic opportunity, led news coverage to characterize his campaign as a form of southern or economic populism.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-30) Edwards also made his refusal to engage in sustained personal attacks on Democratic opponents part of his campaign style, describing his message as positive and "uplifting".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-32)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
[edit]
Edwards struggled to gain substantial support for much of 2003, but his poll numbers rose sharply in the final weeks before the Iowa caucuses. As recently as November he had been polling in single digits there, and his late momentum was aided by the endorsement of _The Des Moines Register_ and growing crowds at campaign events.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-33) Edwards finished a surprising second in Iowa with 32 percent of state delegate equivalents, behind Kerry's 38 percent and ahead of former front-runner Howard Dean at 18 percent.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-35) One week later in the New Hampshire primary, he finished fourth behind Kerry, Dean and Wesley Clark, with about 12 percent of the vote.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-37)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
During the February 3 contests, Edwards won the South Carolina primary with about 45 percent of the vote, his first statewide victory.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-39) In Oklahoma, he finished narrowly behind Clark, while Kerry won Arizona, Delaware, Missouri, New Mexico and North Dakota.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-41) Kerry then won the February 7 caucuses in Michigan and Washington; Edwards finished third in Michigan and fourth in Washington, having focused more heavily on the approaching contests in the South.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-43)
Edwards subsequently finished second to Kerry in Tennessee and Virginia. In Wisconsin on February 17, he again finished second, receiving about 34 percent to Kerry's 40 percent and Dean's 18 percent.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-45) Dean ended his active campaign the following day, leaving Edwards as Kerry's only remaining major challenger and turning the contest into a two-man race ahead of the ten-state March 2 round.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-47)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
Edwards largely avoided directly attacking Kerry until the final days before Super Tuesday. At a February 26 debate in Los Angeles, he emphasized their differences on trade, special interests and electability and argued that Kerry was too closely identified with Washington.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-48) In the February 29 New York debate, their sharpest exchange of the primary campaign, Edwards explicitly portrayed Kerry as a "Washington insider" and mocked Kerry's proposal for a 120-day review of trade agreements as a "Washington committee" response to families that had lost jobs.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-50)
In the Super Tuesday primaries and caucuses on March 2, Kerry won nine of the ten states voting; the only exception was Vermont, won by the withdrawn Dean.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-52) Edwards came closest in Georgia but failed to win a state and decided to end his campaign. Reports of his impending withdrawal circulated during the evening of March 2, before voting or caucusing had concluded everywhere; he formally suspended his campaign in Raleigh the following day and endorsed Kerry.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-54)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
Because reports of Edwards' impending withdrawal reached Minnesota as the state's caucuses were beginning, it has been suggested that the timing influenced some caucus-goers and may have contributed to the comparatively strong finish of Dennis Kucinich._[citation needed_] Minnesota Public Radio reported that Kerry ultimately received just over half of the preference vote, Edwards 27 percent and Kucinich 17 percent.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-55) Edwards also won a presidential straw poll conducted by the Independence Party of Minnesota._[citation needed_]

## Background and announcement
### Surprise North Carolina win
[edit]
After withdrawing from the race, Edwards went on to win the April 17 Democratic caucuses in his home state ofNorth Carolina, with approximately 51 percent of the preference vote._[citation needed_] The result made him the only Democratic candidate besides Kerry to win nominating contests in two states._[citation needed_]

## Background and announcement
### Vice-Presidential nomination
[edit]
On July 6, 2004, Kerry announced that Edwards would be his running mate.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-71) Early public-opinion polling was generally favorable toward the selection: a CBS News poll found that 52 percent of voters were glad Edwards had been chosen, while Gallup found that 64 percent said the choice reflected favorably on Kerry's ability to make important presidential decisions.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-73) At the same time, Republicans and some commentators highlighted Edwards' relative lack of political and foreign-policy experience; Gallup found that a majority regarded his limited political experience as a weakness, although most of those respondents described it as a minor rather than major weakness.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-75)
The selection also drew strong opposition from several national business associations because of Edwards' career as a trial lawyer and his opposition to restrictions on civil litigation. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business groups said the choice would increase their efforts against the Democratic ticket, particularly on tort reform.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-77) The reaction was not uniform among individual business executives; the Kerry campaign also publicized executives who supported the ticket.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-78)

## Shelia Edwards wins Democratic PSC primary as GOP contest heads to runoff
Winners will advance to this fall’s general elections to determine the balance of power at the utility regulator, which sets Georgia Power’s rates.
(Illustration: By the AJC)
Updated May 20, 2026
Democrats now know who their candidates will be this fall in two high stakes races to decide control of the powerful Georgia Public Service Commission, the state’s top utility regulator.
But Republicans will have to wait a bit longer. One GOP primary is headed to a runoff after Tuesday’s voting, while the other was still to close to call Wednesday afternoon.
In the PSC District 5 Democratic primary, Shelia Edwards won outright over opponents Angelia Pressley and Craig Cupid to advance to this fall’s general election, according to The Associated Press.
Related Story
* * *
In a post on her campaign’s Facebook page Wednesday, Edwards thanked Georgians “for the opportunity to bring ‘service’ back to the heart of the Public Service Commission.”
“I am deeply honored and proud to be your Democratic nominee,” she added.
For Edwards, a veteran of Atlanta city government and Democratic politics, it’s her second victory in a PSC primary. She won the District 3 Democratic primary in 2022, but never got a shot in the general election after a legal challenge to Georgia’s statewide elections for PSC seats postponed the contests.
Edwards campaigned on lowering Georgia Power customers’ monthly electric bills and pushing the utility to add more clean energy to the grid.
On the GOP side in the District 5 PSC primary, Republicans Joshua Tolbert and Bobby Mehan will face each other in a runoff next month to decide the party’s candidate. The runoff is scheduled for June 16.
Tolbert, an engineer and self-proclaimed “nerd,” earned 47% of the vote, good enough to finish first in Tuesday’s primary, but below the 50% threshold needed to avoid a runoff. Mehan, a mediator from Bremen in west Georgia, finished second with 31% of the vote to earn a spot in the runoff. Carolyn Roddy, a telecommunications attorney, finished third.
Related Story
* * *
In the District 3 GOP contest, former Republican PSC member Fitz Johnson was clinging to a narrow lead over Brandon Martin, and the AP had not yet declared a winner Wednesday afternoon.

## Shelia Edwards wins Democratic PSC primary as GOP contest heads to runoff
Johnson served on the commission for more than four years after being appointed by Gov. Brian Kemp, but lost his seat last fall to Democratic Commissioner Peter Hubbard. Johnson’s little-known challenger Martin has a campaign website, but has remained under the radar since launching his campaign.
The Republican winner in District 3 will take on Hubbard this fall. Hubbard ran unopposed in the Democratic primary and automatically advanced to the general election.

## What does the PSC do?
As the state’s top utility regulator, the PSC plays a major role in the lives of most Georgians.
The commission’s five elected members set the rates that Georgia Power, the state’s largest electric utility, can charge its 2.8 million customers. Commissioners also decide how much profit the monopoly utility can earn and the sources it uses to generate electricity.
This cycle, the primaries for the two races have received more attention than usual, largely because of what transpired in the PSC elections last year.
Related Story
* * *
After 20-plus years of GOP dominance on the PSC, Democrats managed to flip two seats in November. The winning Democrats — Hubbard and Alicia Johnson — scored lopsided victories after hammering the Republican incumbents on the campaign trail for raising Georgia Power customers’ bills. Georgia Power’s residential customers had seen their monthly bills increase six times since the start of 2023 because of votes by GOP members of the PSC.
Though Republicans currently hold a narrow 3-to-2 edge, Democrats could snatch control of the commission if they sweep both races this fall.

## What are the key issues in the PSC races?
Power bills and broader affordability concerns are still top of mind for many Georgia voters, along with data centers.
Georgia is a top destination for the electricity-gobbling facilities, but most voters are not pleased about it. According to a new Atlanta Journal-Constitution poll, nearly 53% of Republican primary respondents said they would somewhat or strongly disapprove of a data center being built in their community. More than 75% for Democratic respondents said they would disapprove.
The results come after two recent pledges by Georgia Power to lower bills.
The average residential ratepayer could see their monthly bills shrink by $4.04 starting in June, pending the PSC’s approval of a deal next week.
Related Story
* * *
The utility has also agreed to structure its next rate adjustment — to be proposed in 2028 — to be roughly $8.50 a month less than otherwise would be for residential customers. Still, any decrease in monthly bills resulting from that agreement wouldn’t take effect until 2029.
PSC commissioners are elected statewide, but the candidates themselves must live within the boundaries of the district they’re running in.
District 3 includes Clayton, DeKalb and Fulton counties, and District 5 captures large portions of northwest and west-central Georgia, including parts of western metro Atlanta.
.
Drew Kann is a reporter at The Atlanta Journal-Constitution covering climate change and environmental issues. His passion is for stories that capture how humans are responding to a changing environment. He is a proud graduate of the University of Georgia and Northwestern University, and prior to joining the AJC, he held various roles at CNN.
Kristi Swartz is an AJC contributing writer covering climate change and related matters. She writes about how climate change impacts people’s lives, from extreme weather hitting parts of the state more frequently, to higher electricity bills, insurance premiums and health care expenses.

# Sen. John Edwards wins SC Primary
Francis Marion University political scientist Neal Thigpen says Edwards had to win in his native state, and did so in handsome fashion.Thigpen says second place finisher and Democratic presidential front-runner John Kerry showed well, considering he had not been in South Carolina for four months, until the Democratic candidate debate in Greenville last week.
Kerry won primaries in Missouri, Delaware, Arizona and North Dakota on Tuesday. Clark won in Oklahoma. Fallen front-runner Dean conceded in advance that he was likely to remain winless in the nominating campaign.
The Massachusetts senator was coming off wins in Iowa and New Hampshire and had picked up endorsements from Senator Ernest Hollings and Sixth District Congressman Jim Clyburn. Thigpen says Kerry failed to nurture a network of supporters in South Carolina.
Exactly 269 pledged delegates, or more than 10% of the 2162 needed for the nomination, were at stake in seven states. The count breaks down: Missouri (74), Arizona (55), South Carolina (45), Oklahoma (40), New Mexico (26), Delaware (15) and North Dakota (14).

Edwards' stump speech centered on the theme of "two Americas", contrasting the economic and political opportunities available to wealthy and powerful Americans with those available to working and middle-class families.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-29) The theme, together with Edwards' emphasis on fairness, jobs and economic opportunity, led news coverage to characterize his campaign as a form of southern or economic populism.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-30) Edwards also made his refusal to engage in sustained personal attacks on Democratic opponents part of his campaign style, describing his message as positive and "uplifting".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-32)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
[edit]
Edwards struggled to gain substantial support for much of 2003, but his poll numbers rose sharply in the final weeks before the Iowa caucuses. As recently as November he had been polling in single digits there, and his late momentum was aided by the endorsement of _The Des Moines Register_ and growing crowds at campaign events.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-33) Edwards finished a surprising second in Iowa with 32 percent of state delegate equivalents, behind Kerry's 38 percent and ahead of former front-runner Howard Dean at 18 percent.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-35) One week later in the New Hampshire primary, he finished fourth behind Kerry, Dean and Wesley Clark, with about 12 percent of the vote.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-37)
texts.6:
## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
During the February 3 contests, Edwards won the South Carolina primary with about 45 percent of the vote, his first statewide victory.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-39) In Oklahoma, he finished narrowly behind Clark, while Kerry won Arizona, Delaware, Missouri, New Mexico and North Dakota.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-41) Kerry then won the February 7 caucuses in Michigan and Washington; Edwards finished third in Michigan and fourth in Washington, having focused more heavily on the approaching contests in the South.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-43)
Edwards subsequently finished second to Kerry in Tennessee and Virginia. In Wisconsin on February 17, he again finished second, receiving about 34 percent to Kerry's 40 percent and Dean's 18 percent.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-45) Dean ended his active campaign the following day, leaving Edwards as Kerry's only remaining major challenger and turning the contest into a two-man race ahead of the ten-state March 2 round.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-47)
texts.7:
## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
Edwards largely avoided directly attacking Kerry until the final days before Super Tuesday. At a February 26 debate in Los Angeles, he emphasized their differences on trade, special interests and electability and argued that Kerry was too closely identified with Washington.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-48) In the February 29 New York debate, their sharpest exchange of the primary campaign, Edwards explicitly portrayed Kerry as a "Washington insider" and mocked Kerry's proposal for a 120-day review of trade agreements as a "Washington committee" response to families that had lost jobs.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-50)
In the Super Tuesday primaries and caucuses on March 2, Kerry won nine of the ten states voting; the only exception was Vermont, won by the withdrawn Dean.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-52) Edwards came closest in Georgia but failed to win a state and decided to end his campaign. Reports of his impending withdrawal circulated during the evening of March 2, before voting or caucusing had concluded everywhere; he formally suspended his campaign in Raleigh the following day and endorsed Kerry.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-54)
texts.8:
## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
Because reports of Edwards' impending withdrawal reached Minnesota as the state's caucuses were beginning, it has been suggested that the timing influenced some caucus-goers and may have contributed to the comparatively strong finish of Dennis Kucinich._[citation needed_] Minnesota Public Radio reported that Kerry ultimately received just over half of the preference vote, Edwards 27 percent and Kucinich 17 percent.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-55) Edwards also won a presidential straw poll conducted by the Independence Party of Minnesota._[citation needed_]
Key results are shown below. The percentages are rounded to whole numbers. ## Background and announcement
### Vice-Presidential nomination
[edit]
On July 6, 2004, Kerry announced that Edwards would be his running mate.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-71) Early public-opinion polling was generally favorable toward the selection: a CBS News poll found that 52 percent of voters were glad Edwards had been chosen, while Gallup found that 64 percent said the choice reflected favorably on Kerry's ability to make important presidential decisions.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-73) At the same time, Republicans and some commentators highlighted Edwards' relative lack of political and foreign-policy experience; Gallup found that a majority regarded his limited political experience as a weakness, although most of those respondents described it as a minor rather than major weakness.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-75)
The selection also drew strong opposition from several national business associations because of Edwards' career as a trial lawyer and his opposition to restrictions on civil litigation. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business groups said the choice would increase their efforts against the Democratic ticket, particularly on tort reform.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-77) The reaction was not uniform among individual business executives; the Kerry campaign also publicized executives who supported the ticket.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-78)

# Sen. John Edwards wins SC Primary
Francis Marion University political scientist Neal Thigpen says Edwards had to win in his native state, and did so in handsome fashion.Thigpen says second place finisher and Democratic presidential front-runner John Kerry showed well, considering he had not been in South Carolina for four months, until the Democratic candidate debate in Greenville last week.
Kerry won primaries in Missouri, Delaware, Arizona and North Dakota on Tuesday. Clark won in Oklahoma. Fallen front-runner Dean conceded in advance that he was likely to remain winless in the nominating campaign.
The Massachusetts senator was coming off wins in Iowa and New Hampshire and had picked up endorsements from Senator Ernest Hollings and Sixth District Congressman Jim Clyburn. Thigpen says Kerry failed to nurture a network of supporters in South Carolina.
Exactly 269 pledged delegates, or more than 10% of the 2162 needed for the nomination, were at stake in seven states. The count breaks down: Missouri (74), Arizona (55), South Carolina (45), Oklahoma (40), New Mexico (26), Delaware (15) and North Dakota (14).

## Shelia Edwards wins Democratic PSC primary as GOP contest heads to runoff
Winners will advance to this fall’s general elections to determine the balance of power at the utility regulator, which sets Georgia Power’s rates.
(Illustration: By the AJC)
Updated May 20, 2026
Democrats now know who their candidates will be this fall in two high stakes races to decide control of the powerful Georgia Public Service Commission, the state’s top utility regulator.
But Republicans will have to wait a bit longer. One GOP primary is headed to a runoff after Tuesday’s voting, while the other was still to close to call Wednesday afternoon.
In the PSC District 5 Democratic primary, Shelia Edwards won outright over opponents Angelia Pressley and Craig Cupid to advance to this fall’s general election, according to The Associated Press.
Related Story
* * *
In a post on her campaign’s Facebook page Wednesday, Edwards thanked Georgians “for the opportunity to bring ‘service’ back to the heart of the Public Service Commission.”
“I am deeply honored and proud to be your Democratic nominee,” she added.
For Edwards, a veteran of Atlanta city government and Democratic politics, it’s her second victory in a PSC primary. She won the District 3 Democratic primary in 2022, but never got a shot in the general election after a legal challenge to Georgia’s statewide elections for PSC seats postponed the contests.
Edwards campaigned on lowering Georgia Power customers’ monthly electric bills and pushing the utility to add more clean energy to the grid.
On the GOP side in the District 5 PSC primary, Republicans Joshua Tolbert and Bobby Mehan will face each other in a runoff next month to decide the party’s candidate. The runoff is scheduled for June 16.
Tolbert, an engineer and self-proclaimed “nerd,” earned 47% of the vote, good enough to finish first in Tuesday’s primary, but below the 50% threshold needed to avoid a runoff. Mehan, a mediator from Bremen in west Georgia, finished second with 31% of the vote to earn a spot in the runoff. Carolyn Roddy, a telecommunications attorney, finished third.
Related Story
* * *
In the District 3 GOP contest, former Republican PSC member Fitz Johnson was clinging to a narrow lead over Brandon Martin, and the AP had not yet declared a winner Wednesday afternoon.

## Shelia Edwards wins Democratic PSC primary as GOP contest heads to runoff
Johnson served on the commission for more than four years after being appointed by Gov. Brian Kemp, but lost his seat last fall to Democratic Commissioner Peter Hubbard. Johnson’s little-known challenger Martin has a campaign website, but has remained under the radar since launching his campaign.
The Republican winner in District 3 will take on Hubbard this fall. Hubbard ran unopposed in the Democratic primary and automatically advanced to the general election.

## What does the PSC do?
As the state’s top utility regulator, the PSC plays a major role in the lives of most Georgians.
The commission’s five elected members set the rates that Georgia Power, the state’s largest electric utility, can charge its 2.8 million customers. Commissioners also decide how much profit the monopoly utility can earn and the sources it uses to generate electricity.
This cycle, the primaries for the two races have received more attention than usual, largely because of what transpired in the PSC elections last year.
Related Story
* * *
After 20-plus years of GOP dominance on the PSC, Democrats managed to flip two seats in November. The winning Democrats — Hubbard and Alicia Johnson — scored lopsided victories after hammering the Republican incumbents on the campaign trail for raising Georgia Power customers’ bills. Georgia Power’s residential customers had seen their monthly bills increase six times since the start of 2023 because of votes by GOP members of the PSC.
Though Republicans currently hold a narrow 3-to-2 edge, Democrats could snatch control of the commission if they sweep both races this fall.

## What are the key issues in the PSC races?
Power bills and broader affordability concerns are still top of mind for many Georgia voters, along with data centers.
Georgia is a top destination for the electricity-gobbling facilities, but most voters are not pleased about it. According to a new Atlanta Journal-Constitution poll, nearly 53% of Republican primary respondents said they would somewhat or strongly disapprove of a data center being built in their community. More than 75% for Democratic respondents said they would disapprove.
The results come after two recent pledges by Georgia Power to lower bills.
The average residential ratepayer could see their monthly bills shrink by $4.04 starting in June, pending the PSC’s approval of a deal next week.
Related Story
* * *
The utility has also agreed to structure its next rate adjustment — to be proposed in 2028 — to be roughly $8.50 a month less than otherwise would be for residential customers. Still, any decrease in monthly bills resulting from that agreement wouldn’t take effect until 2029.
PSC commissioners are elected statewide, but the candidates themselves must live within the boundaries of the district they’re running in.
District 3 includes Clayton, DeKalb and Fulton counties, and District 5 captures large portions of northwest and west-central Georgia, including parts of western metro Atlanta.

## Background and announcement
Edwards' stump speech centered on the theme of "two Americas", contrasting the economic and political opportunities available to wealthy and powerful Americans with those available to working and middle-class families.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-29) The theme, together with Edwards' emphasis on fairness, jobs and economic opportunity, led news coverage to characterize his campaign as a form of southern or economic populism.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-30) Edwards also made his refusal to engage in sustained personal attacks on Democratic opponents part of his campaign style, describing his message as positive and "uplifting".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-32)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
[edit]
Edwards struggled to gain substantial support for much of 2003, but his poll numbers rose sharply in the final weeks before the Iowa caucuses. As recently as November he had been polling in single digits there, and his late momentum was aided by the endorsement of _The Des Moines Register_ and growing crowds at campaign events.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-33) Edwards finished a surprising second in Iowa with 32 percent of state delegate equivalents, behind Kerry's 38 percent and ahead of former front-runner Howard Dean at 18 percent.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-35) One week later in the New Hampshire primary, he finished fourth behind Kerry, Dean and Wesley Clark, with about 12 percent of the vote.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-37)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
During the February 3 contests, Edwards won the South Carolina primary with about 45 percent of the vote, his first statewide victory.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-39) In Oklahoma, he finished narrowly behind Clark, while Kerry won Arizona, Delaware, Missouri, New Mexico and North Dakota.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-41) Kerry then won the February 7 caucuses in Michigan and Washington; Edwards finished third in Michigan and fourth in Washington, having focused more heavily on the approaching contests in the South.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-43)
Edwards subsequently finished second to Kerry in Tennessee and Virginia. In Wisconsin on February 17, he again finished second, receiving about 34 percent to Kerry's 40 percent and Dean's 18 percent.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-45) Dean ended his active campaign the following day, leaving Edwards as Kerry's only remaining major challenger and turning the contest into a two-man race ahead of the ten-state March 2 round.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-47)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
Edwards largely avoided directly attacking Kerry until the final days before Super Tuesday. At a February 26 debate in Los Angeles, he emphasized their differences on trade, special interests and electability and argued that Kerry was too closely identified with Washington.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-48) In the February 29 New York debate, their sharpest exchange of the primary campaign, Edwards explicitly portrayed Kerry as a "Washington insider" and mocked Kerry's proposal for a 120-day review of trade agreements as a "Washington committee" response to families that had lost jobs.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-50)
In the Super Tuesday primaries and caucuses on March 2, Kerry won nine of the ten states voting; the only exception was Vermont, won by the withdrawn Dean.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-52) Edwards came closest in Georgia but failed to win a state and decided to end his campaign. Reports of his impending withdrawal circulated during the evening of March 2, before voting or caucusing had concluded everywhere; he formally suspended his campaign in Raleigh the following day and endorsed Kerry.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-54)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
Because reports of Edwards' impending withdrawal reached Minnesota as the state's caucuses were beginning, it has been suggested that the timing influenced some caucus-goers and may have contributed to the comparatively strong finish of Dennis Kucinich._[citation needed_] Minnesota Public Radio reported that Kerry ultimately received just over half of the preference vote, Edwards 27 percent and Kucinich 17 percent.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-55) Edwards also won a presidential straw poll conducted by the Independence Party of Minnesota._[citation needed_]

## Background and announcement
### Surprise North Carolina win
[edit]
After withdrawing from the race, Edwards went on to win the April 17 Democratic caucuses in his home state ofNorth Carolina, with approximately 51 percent of the preference vote._[citation needed_] The result made him the only Democratic candidate besides Kerry to win nominating contests in two states._[citation needed_]

## Background and announcement
### Vice-Presidential nomination
[edit]
On July 6, 2004, Kerry announced that Edwards would be his running mate.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-71) Early public-opinion polling was generally favorable toward the selection: a CBS News poll found that 52 percent of voters were glad Edwards had been chosen, while Gallup found that 64 percent said the choice reflected favorably on Kerry's ability to make important presidential decisions.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-73) At the same time, Republicans and some commentators highlighted Edwards' relative lack of political and foreign-policy experience; Gallup found that a majority regarded his limited political experience as a weakness, although most of those respondents described it as a minor rather than major weakness.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-75)
The selection also drew strong opposition from several national business associations because of Edwards' career as a trial lawyer and his opposition to restrictions on civil litigation. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business groups said the choice would increase their efforts against the Democratic ticket, particularly on tort reform.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-77) The reaction was not uniform among individual business executives; the Kerry campaign also publicized executives who supported the ticket.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-78)

# Sen. John Edwards wins SC Primary
Francis Marion University political scientist Neal Thigpen says Edwards had to win in his native state, and did so in handsome fashion.Thigpen says second place finisher and Democratic presidential front-runner John Kerry showed well, considering he had not been in South Carolina for four months, until the Democratic candidate debate in Greenville last week.
Kerry won primaries in Missouri, Delaware, Arizona and North Dakota on Tuesday. Clark won in Oklahoma. Fallen front-runner Dean conceded in advance that he was likely to remain winless in the nominating campaign.
The Massachusetts senator was coming off wins in Iowa and New Hampshire and had picked up endorsements from Senator Ernest Hollings and Sixth District Congressman Jim Clyburn. Thigpen says Kerry failed to nurture a network of supporters in South Carolina.
Exactly 269 pledged delegates, or more than 10% of the 2162 needed for the nomination, were at stake in seven states. The count breaks down: Missouri (74), Arizona (55), South Carolina (45), Oklahoma (40), New Mexico (26), Delaware (15) and North Dakota (14).

The **Clemson Tigers football** program are the American football team at Clemson University. The Tigers compete in the NCAA Division IFootball Bowl Subdivision (FBS) of the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) of the Atlantic Coast Conference (ACC).

Formed in 1896, the program has an all-time record of 804–473–44,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-2) with a bowl record of 27–23. Clemson was a College Football Playoff finalist in 2015, 2016, 2018, and 2019, defeating Alabama in both 2016 and 2018 to secure the national title. Clemson has had six undefeated seasons (including the first-ever 15–0 team), boasted six consecutive playoff appearances from 2015 to 2021, and retains 27 conference championships, including 8 since 2011. Its alumni include over 100 All-Americans, 17 Academic All-Americans and over 250 players in the National Football League.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-4) Clemson has had eight members inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame: players Banks McFadden, Terry Kinard, Jeff Davis, and C. J. Spiller along with coaches John Heisman, Jess Neely, Frank Howard, and Danny Ford.

Clemson is one of the founding members of the ACC and holds 22 ACC titles, the most of any member. Its 28 total conference titles, including six consecutive ACC titles from 2015 to 2020, are the most of any ACC school. Clemson's most recent ACC title came in 2024, against SMU. Clemson's streak of eleven consecutive 10-win seasons from 2011-2022 ranked second in active streaks behind the Alabama Crimson Tide, coming to an end after Clemson's 2023 season where they finished with a 9–4 record.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-6) Among its eight undefeated regular seasons, Clemson has been crowned national champion 3 times. Clemson was named poll-era national champion and finished with its third perfect season with a win over Nebraska in the 1982 Orange Bowl. Clemson was the National Championship Finalist Runner-up with a 14–1 record in 2015 before winning the National Title over No. 1 Alabama in college football's first National Championship rematch in 2016, and again in 2018. However, Clemson then lost the next year to the undefeated LSU Tigers in the 2020 College Football Playoff National Championship 25-42. The Tigers have 46 bowl appearances, 20 of which are among the [New Year's Six](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Year's_Six "New Year's Six") Bowls, including nine during the "Big Four" era. Clemson has 34 finishes in the final top 25 in the modern era and it finished in either the Associated Press final poll or the coaches' final poll a combined 59 times since 1939.
The Tigers play their home games in Memorial Stadium on the university's Clemson, South Carolina campus. The stadium's nickname, "Death Valley" was coined in 1948 by Presbyterian College head coach Lonnie McMillan after his teams were routinely defeated there. Memorial Stadium is among the largest stadiums in college football.
Walter Riggs, the "father of Clemson football"

Walter Riggs, often regarded as the "father of Clemson football," brought the sport to Clemson from the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Alabama (now Auburn University). The team's first game, played on Halloween 1896, resulted in a 2–1 record for the inaugural season. Riggs influenced the choice of the team mascot and colors. The Tigers’ early success included their first undefeated season in 1900 under coach John W. Heisman, who led the team to a 19–3–2 record. Heisman’s coaching set a precedent for excellence and innovation.
During the mid-20th century, the program experienced substantial growth under Frank Howard, who coached from 1940 to 1969. Howard's tenure saw Clemson win two Southern Conference championships and six ACC championships. Known for his colorful personality and imaginative storytelling, Howard integrated various offensive formations. His legacy includes the tradition of rubbing "Howard's Rock" before home games and the naming of the playing field at Memorial Stadium as "Frank Howard Field" in 1974.
The late 20th century and early 21st century saw the football program navigate through challenges and successes under multiple head coaches. Danny Ford led the Tigers to their first national championship in 1981, achieving an undefeated season. Ford's era was marked by NCAA sanctions due to recruiting violations, which impacted the program's reputation and success. Ken Hatfield, Ford’s successor, focused on cleaning up the program's image but faced criticism from fans, leading to his resignation. Subsequent coaches, including Tommy West, struggled to achieve consistent success until the hiring of Tommy Bowden in 1999, who maintained bowl eligibility every season, but failed to secure an ACC championship.
Coach Dabo Swinney

The modern era is defined by the leadership of Dabo Swinney, who became head coach in 2008. Swinney revitalized the program, leading the Tigers to multiple ACC championships and two national titles in 2016 and 2018. His tenure has been characterized by significant achievements, including the establishment of Clemson as a perennial contender in the College Football Playoff. Swinney’s ability to recruit and develop talent, combined with strategic hires like offensive coordinator Chad Morris and defensive coordinator Brent Venables, has sustained Clemson’s success. Notably, under Swinney, Clemson became the first team since 1897 to finish a season 15–0. In 2022, Clemson defeated Syracuse 27–21, extending the Tigers' home winning streak to 38, a new ACC record.

Clemson claims three national championships. In 1981 they finished as the only undefeated team with a 22–15 victory over the No. 4 Nebraska Cornhuskers in the 1982 Orange Bowl, and were named the national champions[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-7) by all major four consensus selectors [[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-8) (AP, Coaches, FWAA, and NFF). As of 2018, the Tiger baseball team has posted a combined 32 ACC regular season and tournament championships (the most in the conference), 43 NCAA Tournament appearances, 17 NCAA Regional Titles, four NCAA Super Regional titles, and 12 College World Series appearances. Much of the baseball program's success occurred under Bill Wilhelm during his 35 seasons as Clemson's head coach. Erik Bakich is the Tigers' current head coach, having replaced Monte Lee after the conclusion of the 2022 season.

The Clemson men's basketball team has qualified for the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_men's_basketball_tournament "NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament") 13 times, and reached the Sweet 16 four times and the Elite Eight once. They are currently coached by Brad Brownell since 2010.
The Clemson women's basketball team began in 1975, and saw its biggest success in the late 1980s and 1990s. The Tigers reached the NCAA Elite Eight in 1991, and the Sweet Sixteen three times (1989, 1990, 1999). Women's basketball won two [ACC Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "ACC women's basketball tournament") championships in 1996 and 1999, and the regular season title in 1981. The team is currently coached by Amanda Butler.
The Tigers take the field by running down the hill in Memorial Stadium's east end zone, 2006.
Clemson has three national championships in football, the most recent coming in 2018 with a victory over Alabama 44–16 in the 2019 College Football Playoff National Championship. Clemson has appeared in the last six playoffs and won two national championships during those visits. The Tigers also possess the most Atlantic Coast Conference championships with 20, including winning the last six.
It has also won greater than 60% of its games, placing it in the top 25 on the all-time winning percentage list. Clemson also won two Southern Conference titles before joining the ACC. The 1981 squad, led by Head Coach Danny Ford, became the first athletic team in school history to win a national championship. Clemson defeated Nebraska 22–15 in the Orange Bowl in Miami, Florida, to win the 1981 NCAA Football National Championship. Stars of the game included Homer Jordan (QB) and Perry Tuttle (WR). Clemson finished the year 12–0 and ranked #1 in the Associated Press and Coaches polls.

Some of the most notable coaching names in Clemson football history are John Heisman (who also coached at Akron, Auburn, Georgia Tech, Penn, Washington & Jefferson, and Rice; the Heisman Trophy is named after him), Jess Neely, Frank Howard (whom the playing field at Death Valley is named after), and Danny Ford. After Tommy Bowden resigned midseason on October 13, 2008, Dabo Swinney took over as interim head coach.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-ESPN-13) On December 1, 2008, Swinney was named head coach of the Clemson Tigers football team.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-14)
Before each home game, the team ends pre-game warm ups and proceeds to the locker room. With five minutes to go before game time, three buses leave the street behind the West Endzone carrying the Clemson football players. The buses pull to a stop at the gate in front of The Hill, and the Tigers gather at the top, where each player proceeds to rub "Howard's Rock", which is an imported rock from Death Valley, California that was presented to Frank Howard in 1967. While Tiger Rag is played and a cannon sounds, the Tigers run down the hill onto the field in front of over 83,000 screaming fans. This tradition has been dubbed "The most exciting 25 seconds in college football" by sportscaster Brent Musburger.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-15)

The Tiger men's golf team have a tradition of being among the best in the ACC and the nation, having won several ACC titles and regularly qualifying for the NCAA Tournament. In 2003, Clemson defeated Oklahoma State to win its first [National Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Men's_Golf_Championships "NCAA Division I Men's Golf Championships") in golf and the 4th overall for the school.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-Golf_2003_NC-16) In addition to that victory, Clemson also won the ACC and NCAA East Regional titles that year, making the Tigers the first program in NCAA history to win its conference, regional, and national championship tournaments in the same year.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-Golf_2003_NC-16) Clemson has also won eight regional titles since the NCAA adopted the regional tournament format in 1989, with their most recent win coming in [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_NCAA_Division_I_men's_golf_championship "2024 NCAA Division I men's golf championship").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-MG-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-18) Two Tigers have won individual NCAA Championships: Charles Warren in 1997 and Turk Pettit in 2021.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-MG-17)2009 U.S. Open champion Lucas Glover also played golf at Clemson.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-19)

### Discontinued varsity sports
Swimming & Diving  
The Tigers men's swimming & diving team was established in 1919, and won the Southern Conference championship in 1939, and the ACC team championship in 1986. The women's swimming & diving team began in 1975, and won 4 ACC championships (1987, 1988, 1989, 1997), and Mitzi Kremer won 4 NCAA championships. Both swimming teams and men's diving were discontinued after the 2012 season, and women's diving was discontinued after 2017.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlackman_et_al.2013209%E2%80%93217-35)
Wrestling  
Wrestling at Clemson University was discontinued in 1995, despite the success of the program, due to financial shortages from Tiger Athletics' funding from the university. The wrestling program began in 1975 winning the ACC title as a team under coach Eddie Griffin in 1991. The Tiger wrestling program produced eight All-Americans, two NCAA Champions, and a finish at the NCAA Championships as high as 7th in 1994.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-36)Noel Loban won Clemson's first national title in 1980, and went on to win a bronze medal in the 1984 Olympics. Sammie Henson is a former standout at Clemson, as one of the most accomplished Tiger wrestlers, with 1993 and 1994 NCAA Champion titles, who eventually earned a 2000 Olympics silver medal and became a World Champion in 1998 in freestyle wrestling.

The **Clemson Tigers football** program are the American football team at Clemson University. The Tigers compete in the NCAA Division IFootball Bowl Subdivision (FBS) of the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) of the Atlantic Coast Conference (ACC).
texts.2: Formed in 1896, the program has an all-time record of 804–473–44,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-2) with a bowl record of 27–23. Clemson was a College Football Playoff finalist in 2015, 2016, 2018, and 2019, defeating Alabama in both 2016 and 2018 to secure the national title. Clemson has had six undefeated seasons (including the first-ever 15–0 team), boasted six consecutive playoff appearances from 2015 to 2021, and retains 27 conference championships, including 8 since 2011. Its alumni include over 100 All-Americans, 17 Academic All-Americans and over 250 players in the National Football League.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-4) Clemson has had eight members inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame: players Banks McFadden, Terry Kinard, Jeff Davis, and C. J. Spiller along with coaches John Heisman, Jess Neely, Frank Howard, and Danny Ford.
texts.3:
Clemson is one of the founding members of the ACC and holds 22 ACC titles, the most of any member. Its 28 total conference titles, including six consecutive ACC titles from 2015 to 2020, are the most of any ACC school. Clemson's most recent ACC title came in 2024, against SMU. Clemson's streak of eleven consecutive 10-win seasons from 2011-2022 ranked second in active streaks behind the Alabama Crimson Tide, coming to an end after Clemson's 2023 season where they finished with a 9–4 record.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-6) Among its eight undefeated regular seasons, Clemson has been crowned national champion 3 times. Clemson was named poll-era national champion and finished with its third perfect season with a win over Nebraska in the 1982 Orange Bowl. Clemson was the National Championship Finalist Runner-up with a 14–1 record in 2015 before winning the National Title over No. 1 Alabama in college football's first National Championship rematch in 2016, and again in 2018. However, Clemson then lost the next year to the undefeated LSU Tigers in the 2020 College Football Playoff National Championship 25-42. The Tigers have 46 bowl appearances, 20 of which are among the [New Year's Six](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Year's_Six "New Year's Six") Bowls, including nine during the "Big Four" era. Clemson has 34 finishes in the final top 25 in the modern era and it finished in either the Associated Press final poll or the coaches' final poll a combined 59 times since 1939.
The Tigers play their home games in Memorial Stadium on the university's Clemson, South Carolina campus. The stadium's nickname, "Death Valley" was coined in 1948 by Presbyterian College head coach Lonnie McMillan after his teams were routinely defeated there. Memorial Stadium is among the largest stadiums in college football.
Walter Riggs, the "father of Clemson football"
texts.4:
Walter Riggs, often regarded as the "father of Clemson football," brought the sport to Clemson from the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Alabama (now Auburn University). The team's first game, played on Halloween 1896, resulted in a 2–1 record for the inaugural season. Riggs influenced the choice of the team mascot and colors. The Tigers’ early success included their first undefeated season in 1900 under coach John W. Heisman, who led the team to a 19–3–2 record. Heisman’s coaching set a precedent for excellence and innovation.
During the mid-20th century, the program experienced substantial growth under Frank Howard, who coached from 1940 to 1969. Howard's tenure saw Clemson win two Southern Conference championships and six ACC championships. Known for his colorful personality and imaginative storytelling, Howard integrated various offensive formations. His legacy includes the tradition of rubbing "Howard's Rock" before home games and the naming of the playing field at Memorial Stadium as "Frank Howard Field" in 1974.
The late 20th century and early 21st century saw the football program navigate through challenges and successes under multiple head coaches. Danny Ford led the Tigers to their first national championship in 1981, achieving an undefeated season. Ford's era was marked by NCAA sanctions due to recruiting violations, which impacted the program's reputation and success. Ken Hatfield, Ford’s successor, focused on cleaning up the program's image but faced criticism from fans, leading to his resignation. Subsequent coaches, including Tommy West, struggled to achieve consistent success until the hiring of Tommy Bowden in 1999, who maintained bowl eligibility every season, but failed to secure an ACC championship.
Coach Dabo Swinney
texts.5: The modern era is defined by the leadership of Dabo Swinney, who became head coach in 2008. Swinney revitalized the program, leading the Tigers to multiple ACC championships and two national titles in 2016 and 2018. His tenure has been characterized by significant achievements, including the establishment of Clemson as a perennial contender in the College Football Playoff. Swinney’s ability to recruit and develop talent, combined with strategic hires like offensive coordinator Chad Morris and defensive coordinator Brent Venables, has sustained Clemson’s success. Notably, under Swinney, Clemson became the first team since 1897 to finish a season 15–0. In 2022, Clemson defeated Syracuse 27–21, extending the Tigers' home winning streak to 38, a new ACC record.

With five minutes to go before game time, three buses leave the street behind the West Endzone carrying the Clemson football players. The buses pull to a stop at the gate in front of The Hill, and the Tigers gather at the top, where each player proceeds to rub "Howard's Rock", which is an imported rock from Death Valley, California that was presented to Frank Howard in 1967. While Tiger Rag is played and a cannon sounds, the Tigers run down the hill onto the field in front of over 83,000 screaming fans. This tradition has been dubbed "The most exciting 25 seconds in college football" by sportscaster Brent Musburger.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-15)
texts.6: The Tiger men's golf team have a tradition of being among the best in the ACC and the nation, having won several ACC titles and regularly qualifying for the NCAA Tournament. In 2003, Clemson defeated Oklahoma State to win its first [National Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Men's_Golf_Championships "NCAA Division I Men's Golf Championships") in golf and the 4th overall for the school.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-Golf_2003_NC-16) In addition to that victory, Clemson also won the ACC and NCAA East Regional titles that year, making the Tigers the first program in NCAA history to win its conference, regional, and national championship tournaments in the same year.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-Golf_2003_NC-16) Clemson has also won eight regional titles since the NCAA adopted the regional tournament format in 1989, with their most recent win coming in [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_NCAA_Division_I_men's_golf_championship "2024 NCAA Division I men's golf championship").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-MG-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-18) Two Tigers have won individual NCAA Championships: Charles Warren in 1997 and Turk Pettit in 2021.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-MG-17)2009 U.S. Open champion Lucas Glover also played golf at Clemson.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-19)

### Discontinued varsity sports
Swimming & Diving  
The Tigers men's swimming & diving team was established in 1919, and won the Southern Conference championship in 1939, and the ACC team championship in 1986. The women's swimming & diving team began in 1975, and won 4 ACC championships (1987, 1988, 1989, 1997), and Mitzi Kremer won 4 NCAA championships. Both swimming teams and men's diving were discontinued after the 2012 season, and women's diving was discontinued after 2017.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlackman_et_al.2013209%E2%80%93217-35)
Wrestling  
Wrestling at Clemson University was discontinued in 1995, despite the success of the program, due to financial shortages from Tiger Athletics' funding from the university. The wrestling program began in 1975 winning the ACC title as a team under coach Eddie Griffin in 1991. The Tiger wrestling program produced eight All-Americans, two NCAA Champions, and a finish at the NCAA Championships as high as 7th in 1994.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-36)Noel Loban won Clemson's first national title in 1980, and went on to win a bronze medal in the 1984 Olympics. Sammie Henson is a former standout at Clemson, as one of the most accomplished Tiger wrestlers, with 1993 and 1994 NCAA Champion titles, who eventually earned a 2000 Olympics silver medal and became a World Champion in 1998 in freestyle wrestling.

The **Clemson Tigers football** program are the American football team at Clemson University. The Tigers compete in the NCAA Division IFootball Bowl Subdivision (FBS) of the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) of the Atlantic Coast Conference (ACC).

Formed in 1896, the program has an all-time record of 804–473–44,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-2) with a bowl record of 27–23. Clemson was a College Football Playoff finalist in 2015, 2016, 2018, and 2019, defeating Alabama in both 2016 and 2018 to secure the national title. Clemson has had six undefeated seasons (including the first-ever 15–0 team), boasted six consecutive playoff appearances from 2015 to 2021, and retains 27 conference championships, including 8 since 2011. Its alumni include over 100 All-Americans, 17 Academic All-Americans and over 250 players in the National Football League.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-4) Clemson has had eight members inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame: players Banks McFadden, Terry Kinard, Jeff Davis, and C. J. Spiller along with coaches John Heisman, Jess Neely, Frank Howard, and Danny Ford.

Clemson is one of the founding members of the ACC and holds 22 ACC titles, the most of any member. Its 28 total conference titles, including six consecutive ACC titles from 2015 to 2020, are the most of any ACC school. Clemson's most recent ACC title came in 2024, against SMU. Clemson's streak of eleven consecutive 10-win seasons from 2011-2022 ranked second in active streaks behind the Alabama Crimson Tide, coming to an end after Clemson's 2023 season where they finished with a 9–4 record.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-6) Among its eight undefeated regular seasons, Clemson has been crowned national champion 3 times. Clemson was named poll-era national champion and finished with its third perfect season with a win over Nebraska in the 1982 Orange Bowl. Clemson was the National Championship Finalist Runner-up with a 14–1 record in 2015 before winning the National Title over No. 1 Alabama in college football's first National Championship rematch in 2016, and again in 2018. However, Clemson then lost the next year to the undefeated LSU Tigers in the 2020 College Football Playoff National Championship 25-42. The Tigers have 46 bowl appearances, 20 of which are among the [New Year's Six](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Year's_Six "New Year's Six") Bowls, including nine during the "Big Four" era. Clemson has 34 finishes in the final top 25 in the modern era and it finished in either the Associated Press final poll or the coaches' final poll a combined 59 times since 1939.
The Tigers play their home games in Memorial Stadium on the university's Clemson, South Carolina campus. The stadium's nickname, "Death Valley" was coined in 1948 by Presbyterian College head coach Lonnie McMillan after his teams were routinely defeated there. Memorial Stadium is among the largest stadiums in college football.
Walter Riggs, the "father of Clemson football"

Walter Riggs, often regarded as the "father of Clemson football," brought the sport to Clemson from the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Alabama (now Auburn University). The team's first game, played on Halloween 1896, resulted in a 2–1 record for the inaugural season. Riggs influenced the choice of the team mascot and colors. The Tigers’ early success included their first undefeated season in 1900 under coach John W. Heisman, who led the team to a 19–3–2 record. Heisman’s coaching set a precedent for excellence and innovation.
During the mid-20th century, the program experienced substantial growth under Frank Howard, who coached from 1940 to 1969. Howard's tenure saw Clemson win two Southern Conference championships and six ACC championships. Known for his colorful personality and imaginative storytelling, Howard integrated various offensive formations. His legacy includes the tradition of rubbing "Howard's Rock" before home games and the naming of the playing field at Memorial Stadium as "Frank Howard Field" in 1974.
The late 20th century and early 21st century saw the football program navigate through challenges and successes under multiple head coaches. Danny Ford led the Tigers to their first national championship in 1981, achieving an undefeated season. Ford's era was marked by NCAA sanctions due to recruiting violations, which impacted the program's reputation and success. Ken Hatfield, Ford’s successor, focused on cleaning up the program's image but faced criticism from fans, leading to his resignation. Subsequent coaches, including Tommy West, struggled to achieve consistent success until the hiring of Tommy Bowden in 1999, who maintained bowl eligibility every season, but failed to secure an ACC championship.
Coach Dabo Swinney

The modern era is defined by the leadership of Dabo Swinney, who became head coach in 2008. Swinney revitalized the program, leading the Tigers to multiple ACC championships and two national titles in 2016 and 2018. His tenure has been characterized by significant achievements, including the establishment of Clemson as a perennial contender in the College Football Playoff. Swinney’s ability to recruit and develop talent, combined with strategic hires like offensive coordinator Chad Morris and defensive coordinator Brent Venables, has sustained Clemson’s success. Notably, under Swinney, Clemson became the first team since 1897 to finish a season 15–0. In 2022, Clemson defeated Syracuse 27–21, extending the Tigers' home winning streak to 38, a new ACC record.

This tradition has been dubbed "The most exciting 25 seconds in college football" by sportscaster Brent Musburger.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-15)

The Tiger men's golf team have a tradition of being among the best in the ACC and the nation, having won several ACC titles and regularly qualifying for the NCAA Tournament. In 2003, Clemson defeated Oklahoma State to win its first [National Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Men's_Golf_Championships "NCAA Division I Men's Golf Championships") in golf and the 4th overall for the school.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-Golf_2003_NC-16) In addition to that victory, Clemson also won the ACC and NCAA East Regional titles that year, making the Tigers the first program in NCAA history to win its conference, regional, and national championship tournaments in the same year.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-Golf_2003_NC-16) Clemson has also won eight regional titles since the NCAA adopted the regional tournament format in 1989, with their most recent win coming in [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_NCAA_Division_I_men's_golf_championship "2024 NCAA Division I men's golf championship").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-MG-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-18) Two Tigers have won individual NCAA Championships: Charles Warren in 1997 and Turk Pettit in 2021.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-MG-17)2009 U.S. Open champion Lucas Glover also played golf at Clemson.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-19)

### Discontinued varsity sports
Swimming & Diving  
The Tigers men's swimming & diving team was established in 1919, and won the Southern Conference championship in 1939, and the ACC team championship in 1986. The women's swimming & diving team began in 1975, and won 4 ACC championships (1987, 1988, 1989, 1997), and Mitzi Kremer won 4 NCAA championships. Both swimming teams and men's diving were discontinued after the 2012 season, and women's diving was discontinued after 2017.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlackman_et_al.2013209%E2%80%93217-35)
Wrestling  
Wrestling at Clemson University was discontinued in 1995, despite the success of the program, due to financial shortages from Tiger Athletics' funding from the university. The wrestling program began in 1975 winning the ACC title as a team under coach Eddie Griffin in 1991. The Tiger wrestling program produced eight All-Americans, two NCAA Champions, and a finish at the NCAA Championships as high as 7th in 1994.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-36)Noel Loban won Clemson's first national title in 1980, and went on to win a bronze medal in the 1984 Olympics. Sammie Henson is a former standout at Clemson, as one of the most accomplished Tiger wrestlers, with 1993 and 1994 NCAA Champion titles, who eventually earned a 2000 Olympics silver medal and became a World Champion in 1998 in freestyle wrestling.

### Team national championships
[edit]
Clemson University has five team national championships awarded by the NCAA in golf and soccer.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-NC_summary-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-Clemson_United_Wins_Fourth_National_Championship_In_School_History-38) Clemson also claims three Division I Football National Championships, in 1981, 2016, and 2018. These titles were not awarded by the NCAA, but by selectors designated as "major" by the NCAA, such as the AP and Coaches Poll in 1981, and by the College Football Playoff system in 2016 and 2018.
*   **Men's** (8)   
    *   [Golf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Men's_Golf_Championships#Team_titles "NCAA Division I Men's Golf Championships") (1): 2003  
    *   [Soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Men's_Soccer_Championship#Team_titles "NCAA Division I Men's Soccer Championship") (4): [1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Clemson_Tigers_men's_soccer_team "1984 Clemson Tigers men's soccer team"), [1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_Clemson_Tigers_men's_soccer_team "1987 Clemson Tigers men's soccer team"), [2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Clemson_Tigers_men's_soccer_team "2021 Clemson Tigers men's soccer team"), [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Clemson_Tigers_men's_soccer_team "2023 Clemson Tigers men's soccer team")  
    *   Football (3): 1981, 2016, 2018
